## Structural variants (SVs)

![](./img/sv-types.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Structural variants are primary variation I will discuss
- They are large mutations deviating from expected human genome sequence
- SVs types characterize how seq. varies from expected
- DEL: loss of sequence
- DUP: gain of existing seq.
- INV: reversal of order
- INS: gain of novel seq.
- TRANS: sequence misplaced compared to expected
:::

## Large base pair effect size of SVs

![](./img/sv-effect_size.png)

:::notes
- SVs are important because they contribute a large amount of total bp variation per genome
- Estimates vary, but genome.gov estimates >20Mbp of variation on avg.
- However, # SV events small (~25k) compared to SNPs and INDELs
:::

## Disease driving SVs

:::{.center}
:::{.small}

| Mechanism | When | Recurrency | Breakpoint homology | Ex. pathology |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | 
| NAHR | Recombination | Relatively high | Large | Smith–Magenis syndrome; DEL CHR 17, RAI1 |
| NHEJ  | Repair | Low | None or small | Leukemia; FUSION, BCR-ABL |
| BIR | Replication | Low | Small | Temple syndrome; DEL CHR 14 |
| FoSTeS | Replication | Low | Small | Pelizaeus-Merzbacher; DUP CHR X, PLP1 | 

:::
:::

:::notes
- SVs often causes disease
- Especially, neurological, developmental, and cancer diseases
- Therefore, there's clinical incentive to understand SVs:
  - What mechanisms cause them?
  - When do SV mechanisms occur?
  - Do they occur in multiple individuals (recurrency)?
  - Are they pathological?
:::

- When: synthesis, recombination, or repair

## SV mechanism research gaps

<br>

:::{.center}

1. Calling dependent SVs
2. Calling SVs using sequencing and mechanism models jointly
3. Mechanism-pathology association

:::

- :::notes
- For each section, I want to pose potential research gaps to consider throughout and revisit this at the end
- In summary, there's a few gaps related to SV mechs.
- Calling dependent SVs, as we will see many SVs are not independent, yet SV callers typically do not leverage this. Usually analysis is done post-hoc.
- Second, leveraging mechanistic models during the call process is under-investigated and may improve the quality of callsets. Most methods use seq. data only
- Third, the association of mechanisms and pathologies is under-investigated mostly due to limited availability of large disease sample sizes
- So, consider if the papers I discuss support these putative gaps or not
:::


## Allelic homologous recombination

![](./img/recombination.jpg){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
The first mechanism involves recombination process where DNA is exchanged between homologous chromosomes at the same location or allele.
:::

## Non-allelic homologous recombination

![](./img/non-allelic-homologous-recombination.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- However, 'non-allelic' homologous recombination is crossing over at two different sites causing SV
- For ex, 2 homologous chromosomes might line up incorrectly due to repeat homology 
- In the left example, the AB alleles of the 1st chromosome abnormally lines up with the CD alleles of the 2nd chromosome
- This may cause a DEL in one chromosome and a DUP in the other
:::

:::{.small}
:::{.center}

<br>

NAHR SV near RAI1 and nearby genes on CHR 17

<br>

![](./img/smith-magenis-syndrome.jpg){fig-align="center" width="20%"}

:::

:::notes
- Smith-Magenis syndrome is hypothesized to be caused by NAHR nearby the RAI1 gene
- Symptoms include physical and developmental abnormalities

## Segmental duplications drive NAHR

<br>

:::{.center}
:::{.small}

- Segmental duplications (SDs) recruit NAHR
- ~5% of human genome
- High identity (>~95%)
- Large (>~10kbp)


![](./img/segmental-duplication.png)

:::
:::

:::notes
- A canonical homologous element is the segmental duplication
- These are large highly homologous (high seq. similarity) elements
- The area around these elements is known to be a hotspot for NAHR
:::




## NAHR DEL-DUP

![](./img/nahr-del-dup.png)


:::notes
- How exactly does this mechanism work?
- Say we have 2 chromosomes with 2 large, homologous repeats on each
:::

## NAHR DEL-DUP

![](./img/nahr-del-dup-recombination-window.png)

:::notes
- The recombination window might abnormally form like this
- And after crossing over, the top chromosome will only receive 1 repeat copy, while the bottom chr receives an extra third repeat copy
:::

## NAHR DEL-DUP

![](./img/nahr-del-dup-result.png)

## NAHR elements and risk

<br>

:::{.small}
:::{.center}

| Homologous element | Min. Seq. identitiy | Min. length | 
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Segmental duplication (SD) | 90% | 1kbp |
| Long interspersed nuclear element (LINE) | 96% | smaller than 1kbp |
| Human endogenous retro virus (HERV) | 93% | 3kbp | 

<br>


- Risk $\propto$ length, sequence identity, closeness

:::
:::

::: notes
- Beyond SDs, other genomic elements are known to cause SVs via NAHR: LINE and HERV
- The SV risk of NAHR increases as the repeats are larger or more similar
- The SV risk also increases the closer these elments are

:::


## Non-homologous end joining (NHEJ)

![](./img/nhej.webp){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Another mechanism is non-homolgous-end joining
- When DNA broken, then imperfectly repaired
:::

## Chronic myeloid leukemia fusion


:::{.small}
:::{.center}
- NHEJ SV hypothesis (minimal breakpoint homology)
- Recurrency hypothesis: CHR9 and CHR22 regions are physically close

:::
:::

:::notes
- For example, in chronic myeloid leukemia, the tumor driving fusion BCR-ABL is hyp. to be from NHEJ
- Although NHEJ is not typically recurrent, the hypothesis is that CHR9 and CHR22 gene regions are physically close, and suscetible to abnormal repair deriving a fusion event
:::


![](./img/bcr-abl.jpg){fig-align="center"}

## NHEJ example

![](./img/dup-trp.inv-dup.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- A common complex SV formed by NHEJ is a DUP, TRP, DUP event when a replication fork collapses unexpectedly during DNA synthesis
- 1) one replication fork collapses
- 2) the loose end invades another replication fork 
- 3) synthesis begins again
- 4) The second replication collapses and a dsDNA break occurs
- finally, synthesized strand invades the break producing a large copy number gain

:::

## NHEJ summary

<br>

:::{.center}

- Imperfect repair of double strand DNA break
- Minimal homology at breakpoints
- Example: BCR-ABL1 fusion CML
- *Usually* low recurrency

:::

## Break-induced replication (BIR)

<br>

<br>

![](./img/break-induced-replication-DUP.png){fig-align="center"}

<!-- from Mechanisms underlying structural
variant formation in genomic disorders -->

:::notes
- Replication fork collapses
- Abnormal loose end of synth. strand
- Template switch over to previous repeat copy
- Result is a duplication
:::



## Fork stalling and template switching (FoSTeS)

:::{.center}

Template switching during replication

<br>

![](./img/fostes.png){fig-align="center"}

:::

:::notes
- Replication
- Stalling (e.g., secondary structure)
- Lagging strand frees
- Invades another replication fork
:::


## SV mechanisms

<br>

:::{.small}
:::{.center}


| Mechanism | When | Recurrency | Breakpoint homology | Ex. pathology |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| NAHR | Recombination | Relatively high | Large | Smith–Magenis syndrome; DEL on CHR 17, RAI1 gene |
| NHEJ  | Repair | Low | None or small | Chronic Myeloid Leukemia; FUSION of BCR-ABL genes |
| BIR | Replication | Low | Small | Temple syndrome; DEL on CHR 14 |
| FoSTeS | Replication | Low | Small | Pelizaeus-Merzbacher; DUP CHR X, PLP1 gene | 

:::
:::

::: notes
- In summary, NAHR characterized by recurrent events and large breakpoint homology
- Other mechs have low recurrency, homology, and occur during repair or replication

:::

## SV mechanism research gaps

<br>

:::{.center}

1. Calling dependent SVs
2. Calling SVs using sequencing and mechanism models jointly
3. Mechanism-pathology association

:::

:::notes
- Revisting research gaps,
- SVs are not indepdendent
- Often treated independent during calling
- Post-hoc analysis resolves dependence
- Second, calling SVs based on mech models (e.g., breakpoint homology) may increase precision
- Third, quantifying association of mech. and path. would help us understand disease causes
:::

## Dependent SVs and mechanisms

:::{.center}
:::{.small}
- A single NHEJ event may produce multiple SVs
- NAHR rarely produces insertions
- Breakpoint sequence could rule out SV dependence
  - E.g., INS+DEL with large homology at DEL breakpoints
:::


![](./img/nhej.webp){fig-align="center" width="55%"}

:::

:::notes
- As we saw, a single NHEJ event may produce multiple SVs
- NAHR has characteristic homology and SV types
- Although, it would be challenging to resolve NHEJ, BIR, and FoSTeS solely on breakpoints since they all have low homology
:::

## Research gaps

:::{.center}
1. Mobile element detection and inspection
2. Low VAF specialized analysis
:::


:::notes
- Research gaps relative to pop. SV analysis
- Mobile elements cause a significant amount of SVs, yet majority of callers focus on DELs and copy number variants
- Experimental wesults were often sensitive to low VAF.
- Correcting for and addressing low VAF SVs is important since rare SVs are more likley to be pathogenic than common SVs
:::

## SNV-element overlap

::::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}

:::{.small}
- Missense: changes codon -> changes protein sequence
- **pLoF**: predicted loss of function
- **MAPS**: mutability adjusted proportion of singletons
- CpG transition: CG -> TG
- Transversion: Purine (GA) <-> Pyrimidine (CT)

:::

:::
:::{.column width="50%"}
![](./img/gnomad-f1cdefgh.png){fig-align="center" width="90%"}
:::
::::

::: notes
- This was quantified using MAPS: mutability adjusted proportion
- Some other acronyms and terms:
- Missense: SNV changes codon and protein seq.
- pLoF: predicted loss of function
- CpG: special type of SNP
- Transversion is when purine base changes to pyrimidine or vice versa
:::

## MAPS intution

:::{.center}
Is SNV functional class enriched with rare (singleton) events?
:::

![](./img/gnomad-f1cdefgh.png){fig-align="center" width="90%"}

:::notes
- goal of MAPS metric is to test if an SNV func. class enriched with singleton events
- If a class is more rare than expected, then it is constrained
:::

## MAPS

:::{.center}
:::{.small}

- MAPS: Mutability adjusted proportion of singletons
- Aggregate singletons within SNV functional classes (e.g., pLoF or missense)
- MAPS $\approx$ Observed singleton prop. $-\text{ }f$(expected singleton prop.)
- MAPS > 0: more singletons observed than expected
<!-- - Expected: derived from non-coding regions, weighted by mutation rate (freq.) -->

![](./img/maps.png){fig-align="center" width="20%"}

:::
:::

:::notes
- MAPS: Mutability adjusted proportion of singletons
- Aggregate singletons within SNV functional classes (e.g., pLoF or missense)
- MAPS > 0: more singletons observed than expected
- Expected is estimated from non-coding regions and weighted by SNP mutation rates
:::

## pLoF negative selection

:::{.center}

pLoF mutation rates are constrained to be rare 

![](./img/gnomad-f1cdefgh.png){fig-align="center" width="30%"}

:::

:::notes
- So, in summary the high MAPS value showed that LoF variants are constrained to be rare

## LoF annotation-based filtering

![](./img/gnomad-f2ab.png){fig-align="center"}

::: notes

- They developed an annotation-based filter for loss of function variants,called LOFTEE
- Example annotation filters: UTR splice site would not affect the protein seq.
- In summary, LOFTEE filtering agrees with ClinVar annotations and observed AF
- That is, higher AF were more likely to be filtered out as non LoF variants

:::

![](./img/gnomad-f2cd.png){fig-align="center" width="50%"}

## pLoF functional consequences

![](./img/gnomad-f3abcd.png){fig-align="center" width="50%"}

:::notes
- Using their cohort, they developed statistical metric to rank genes constrained to LoF variants
- When applied, the metric isolated essential genes and non-essential genes (like olfactory genes)
:::

## LOEUF

:::{.small}
:::{.center}

- LOEUF: Loss-of-function observed expected upper bound fraction
- Goal: mesaure intolerance to pLoF
- Approach: score genes by pLoF SNV proportion
- Metric: #Obs. pLoF SNVs / #Exp. pLoF SNVs; take upper bound CI

![](./img/loeuf-ex.png){fig-align="center"}

:::
:::

:::notes
- LOEUF metric is "Loss-of-function observed expected upper bound fraction"
- Goal: mesaure intolerance to pLoF
- approach: score genes by pLoF SNV proportion
- value: #Obs. pLoF SNVs / #Exp. pLoF SNVs; take upper bound CI
- A lower value implies a gene constrained to not have LoF variants
- The confidence interval allows better resolution for small and large genes, such as the example in text
:::

## Trait inheritance LOEUF association

:::{.center}
:::{.small}
- Partitioning heritability enrichment
  - \> 1 $\rightarrow$ trait heritability explained by SNVs greater than random chance

![](./img/gnomad-5b.png){fig-align="center" width="70%"}

:::
:::

:::notes
- For trait heritability,
- They compared LOEUF to partitioning heritability enrichment
- heritability enrichment >1 implies trait heritability explained by SNVs is greater than random chance
- Again, the heritability metric is larger for low LOEUF genes
:::


## Trait pLoF SNV association

:::{.center}
:::{.small}
- Null: is trait NOT associated with pLoF variants?
- Schizophrenia and educational attainment previously reported as pLoF associated

:::
:::

![](./img/gnomad-5c.png)

:::notes
- Finally, they tested for trait enrichment of pLoF variants
- Roughly, the null hyp. is that a trait is not associate with LoF variants
- When applied to an external cohort,
- They found that traits like schizophrenia and educational attainment were sig. associated
- Agreeing with previous findings
:::

## DEL breakpoint accuracy

:::{.center}
:::{.small}
- "True" breakpoints: assembly (TIGRA) and long-reads (PacBio)
- Low VAF SV breakpoints less accurate
- Pindel accuracy; likley due to split-read reliance
:::
:::

:::notes
- Breakpoint accuracy was evaluated using assembled contigs and long-reads
- They found low VAF SV breakpoints were less accurate
- Pindel tool had high accuracy; it uses split read evidence only which always includes the junction sequence
:::

## Discordant v split reads

## SV SNP LD

:::{.center}
:::{.small}

- **LD**: linkage disequilibrium
  - $r^2 \approx 1 \rightarrow$ non-random co-occurence
  - $r^2 \approx 0 \rightarrow$ random co-occurence
- Here, LD measured for SVs and nearby SNPs

:::
:::
![](./img/1kg_sv_sr-1e.png){fig-align="center" width="70%"}

:::notes
- Using the linkage disequilibrium metric, they measured co-occurence stats for SVs and nearby SNPs
- If r sq. is high this implies correlation or non-random co-occurence
- Low implies co-occurence seems random
:::

## SV element overlap

- Expected: shuffled SVs intersecting with true elements
- Approaches: i) partial overlap and ii) engulf overlap

![](./img/1kg_sv_sr-2ab.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Next, they analyzed the overlap of SVs and genomic elements
- The expected overlap was computed by shuffling SVs while keeping other elements in-place
- Their supp. methods described two ways to count overlap
- i) partial overlap or
- ii) engulf overlap
:::

## Partial v enguled overlap

<br>

<br>

![](./img/partial-v-engulfed-overlap.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Partial overlap requires only 1 bp overlap
- Engulf overlap requires the entire element to be contained in the SV
- For the following results, partial overlap is reported
:::

## SV partial element overlap

- Log enrichment: $<0 \rightarrow$ less overlap than expected
- RVIS: residual variation intolerance score (functional variant intolernace)
  - $\uparrow RVIS \rightarrow$ $\uparrow$ variant tolerance

![](./img/1kg_sv_sr-2ab.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- The log obs./exp. was computed for various elements
- Another important stat is RVIS: measuring functional variant intolerance
- In summary,
- and left fig.: lower VAF -> higher chance of element overlap
- right: DELs are usually more constrained than other SV types
- in general, constrained regions were negatively enriched with SV overlap
:::

## SV expression association

:::{.center}
:::{.small}

- DUSP22: sig. eQTL variants overlaps TSS and coding seq.
- ZNF43: sig. eQTL variants are upstream coding seq.

:::
:::

![](./img/1kg_sv_sr-2cd.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- For SV-expression association, eQTL was used
- They noticed it was possible for lead eQTL variants to be either
- i) at TSS or (top)
- ii) some small distance away from TSS (bottom)
:::

## SV expression association

:::{.center}
:::{.small}

- eQTL: expression quantitative trait loci
  - Null: no association of SV and gene expression
  - $\downarrow p \rightarrow$ SV associate with gene expression change

:::
:::

![](./img/1kg_sv_sr-2cd.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Briefly, eQTL null is essentially that there is no assication of an SV and gene expression
:::

## LD of lead eQTL SNPs and SVs

:::{.small}
:::{.center}
- Hypothesis: sig. GWAS SNPs associated with SVs
- Denom: # expected SVs in LD with lead eQTL
  - Swap SV into another SV region with similar properties (e.g., VAF)
  - Restrict LD search space to +/- Xbps from TSS
  - Constrain haplotype length ($r^2$ [$\downarrow r^2 \rightarrow \uparrow$ haplotype len.])
  - Is lead eQTL SNP in haplotype length? (yes $\rightarrow+1$)
:::
:::

:::notes
- They tested for enrichment of SVs in LD with lead eQTL
- Found that constraining the haplotype length (r sq.) lead to larger enrichment
- They also observed larger enrichment in larger SVs
- In summary, it's possible that traits associated lead eQTL SNPs may actually explained by SVs
:::

![](./img/1kg_sv_sr-2e.png){fig-align="center"}

## Genotype v haplotype

:::{.center}
:::{.small}
- Genotype: which alleles present and how many?
  - Ex: A/A homozygous SNP at CHR4:123456bp $\rightarrow$ genotype = "1/1"
- Haplotype: which alleles physically linked on singular chromosome?
  - Ex: SNPs at bp 4 (C>A) & 7 (A>C)  are "phased" to same physical chromosome
:::
:::

![](./img/genotype-v-haplotype.webp){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- A side note
- Genotype tell us which alleles are present
- A haplotype tells us which allele are physically linked together on a sinular CHR

# SVs in cancer

## Research gaps

:::{.center}

1. Complex/clustered SV event detection
2. Developing, tuning, and using tools for specific cancer types

:::

:::notes
- Clustered SV events (chromothripsis) tend to occur early in cancer. Therefore, it is important to detect and understand these events
- As we will see, the driver variants vary heavily across tumor types. Yet, pan-cancer analysis is still a popular approach.
- To address heterogenity of different cancer types, developing tumor-specific tools, or tuning them to cancer types seems necessary.
:::

## PCAWG

:::{.center}
Sections

1. Variant caller evaluation
2. Driver mutations
3. Clustered variant events
4. Germline and somatic variant associations
5. Telomere mutations

- i) Variant caller evaluation

## Missing driver investigation

:::{.center}

:::

![](./img/pcawg-3abc.png){fig-align="center"}

- 181 samples did not have driver mutations, so they investigated this and
- i) some samples' drivers were rescued after addressing tumor-in-normal contamination (a)
- ii) for TERT-sensitive cancers many samples depth and purity was estimated insufficient to detect TERT mutations (bc)
- GOTO NEXT
- a) contamination measured by variant allele frequency difference in tumor and normal
- b) Estimated mutation detection sensitivity given purity and depth
- Again, this was only done for samples w/o drivers
- c) TERT detection sensitivity in cancers where TERT is commonly mutated

Sections

## SV types

![](./img/pcawg_sv-1.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- SVs were stratified into 4 groups
- First split is "cut or copy" -> loss/gain in copy number
- Second split is "simple or complex". complex usually has >2  breakpoints
- New SVs worth discussing are 
  - local n-jump: composed of DUPs and INVs
  - Cyclic template INS are copy number gains with shared-chaining breakpoints
:::

## SV tumor frequency

![](./img/pcawg_sv-2.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- The frequency of these types showed a few patterns
- i) (a) Complex/unclassified SVs were most abundant
- ii) (a) DEL and tandem DUP were frequent simple types
- iii) some cancers with only a few samples had high cohort-wise SV count (top value per subplot is # samples)
- subpanels sorted by total SV count
- for panel b), esophagal cancers had a lot DEL, Tandem DUP, and complex SVs. And DELs dominanated highest SV count samples of Ovary
- The remainder of this paper is mostly describing a few categories of complex SVs
:::

## Template insertion SVs

![](./img/pcawg_sv-3abc.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- a) Cycle: the sequence of SV breakpoints that returns to source and the source copy is also gained
- b) Chain: sequence of gains, but no return to source
- c) Bridge: same as cycle, but the source copy is not gained (neutral)
- Sequence path is resolved purely by breakpoints
- Q: how do we know breakpoint chains are not just due to hotspot regions?
- I would be interested to know the mutational burden on these breakpoint regions
:::

## Liver TERT cycles

![](./img/pcawg_sv-3de.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- They observed cycle SV commonly in liver cancers involving the TERT gene
- And hypothesized TERT amplification and inc. telomere resistance may be due to these template insertion cycle events
:::

## Local n-jumps

![](./img/pcawg_sv-4ab.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- For local n-jumps,
- high counts of various jump types occured in different cancers
:::

## Bimodal size distributions

![](./img/pcawg_sv-5ab.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Regarding SV sizes,
- Both DEL and template INS SVs concentrate at two modes: 1kbp and 100kbp
- 1kbp SVs may be due to mobile elements like L1 or SVA
- 100kbp is quite large and not easily explained by mobile elements
:::

## SV properties

![](./img/pcawg_sv-5c.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Looking at some SV features,
- i) DEL and DUP often have opposite median shifts w.r.t features
- ii) interestingly, w.r.t gene intersection small DELs were less likely than random, but large DELs were more likley than random
- NEXT
- star: means significant KS hypothesis test (not-uniform)
- LAD: lamine association domain: associated with nuclear envelope management
- Compared with quantile distribution of random SV placement
:::

## Breakpoint microhomology

![](./img/pcawg_sv-5d.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Looking at breakpoint microhomology
- smaller homology was more commonly observed
- It's unclear if peaks occured at bp sizes > 50 which might be due to mobile elements as we saw in the 1KG papers

![](./img/pcawg_sv-5e.png){fig-align="center"}

- but intuitively, depletion of SVs connecting fragile regions and genes

## SV signatures

![](./img/pcawg_sv-6a.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Using signatures, they abstractly represented SV types
- Some takeaways include
- Tandem DUPs often occur with other SV types
- Chromoplexy events are more often cyclic events rather than chains. Meaning the source chromosome also has copy gain
- INVs are crucial for fold-backs (Breakage fusion bridge)
- Columns: signatures
- Rows: features such as type, size, timing
- Bar: how much SV feature contributes to signature

## Bivalent promoter lead eQTL

:::{.center}

- Bivalent: marked with both active & repressive chromatin marks
:::

![](./img/pcawg_rna-1c.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- An example eQTL was in testicular cancer at a bivalent promoter
- TEKT5: important for sperm mobility and integrity. therefore its expression is important in testes
- This gene is known to be a driver in testicular cancer, likely a regulation swap with other driver genes
- They found eQTLs were at a bivalent promoter.
- Bivalent promoter means the gene is epigentically sensitive to either up/down-regulation

# Gene fusions

## Research gaps

:::{.center}

1. Recurrent fusion caller over multiple samples
2. Resolving fusions as DNA/RNA driven

:::

:::notes
- Now before getting into the papers, I want to pose some research opportunities for fusions
- i) Since recurrent fusions are more likely to be drivers, a multi-sample caller could leverage single from multiple samples to inc. sens beyond 1 sample and find recurrent fusions.
- ii) since fusions could occur solely as RNA events such as post-transcription splicing or read-through transcription, it would be useful to resolve the 2 cases
- DNA mutations are not strictly necessary for fusion genes
- Also, promoter/UTR exchanges may cause dysregulation, not an actual fusion protein
:::


## Fusion benchmarking

:::{.center}
Sections

1. Fusion calling strategy and evaluation
2. Simulation eval.
3. Cancer cell line eval.
:::

:::notes
- First, we will look at a popular fusion benchmarking paper
- It summarizes fusion calling strategies and how evaluation is performed
- Then experiments compare tools in simulated data and real cancer cell line data

:::

## Fusion calling strategy

:::{.center}
- 18 alignment-based methods
- 5 assembly-based methods
:::

![](./img/fusion_bench-1a.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- There are two strategy types to calling fusions
- i) raw read alignemnt (short contigs)
- ii) Transcript assembly then alignment
- the units of fusion evidence are i) discordant/spanning reads and ii) split/junction reads
- Discordant reads are specific to paired-end technology: each mate maps fully to another gene
- Split reads are evidence in single or paired-end read techs: the read partially maps to both genes
:::

## Fusion calling evaluation

![](./img/fusion_bench-1b.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Evaluation is done via classification metrics to both compare tools and select parameters (e.g., min. supporting reads per call)
- Problem: full truth set is typically unknown
- NEXT
- Precision = TP/ \hat{P}
- Recall = TP / P
- F1 combines recall and precision
:::

## Simulated evaluation


![](./img/fusion_bench-2ab.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- However, in simulation the truth set is known
- The performance summary here is that
- read methods outperform the assembly methods (Trinity and Jaffa-assembly)
- most methods performed better with longer read lengths, except SOAPFuse and Fusionhunter (older tools probably tuned to older seq. tech with smaller read lens)
- overall best performers were Arriba, pizzly, STAR-Fusion (highest auPRC)
- and panel b shows higher fusion expression led to higher recall
:::

## Cell line evaluation

:::{.center}
- Experimentally validated fusions from 4/60 cell lines
:::

![](./img/fusion_bench-3ab.png){fig-align="center" width="60%"}

:::notes
- For real data, they started with 4 cell lines that had experimentally validated fusions
- Only showing fusions called by 3 or more methods here
- The key points are
- recall was highest for tools that also performed best in simulated eval
- Only 1 exp. val. fusion found by single method (FusionCatcher) (not shown by figure)
- In panel b,
- left VA is recall of validated fusions, bars
- right VA is precision of ensemble calls (intersection), blue line
- The horizontal axis varies a threshold of caller agreement
- we see that precision asymptotes at about 10 caller agreement
- recall falls off for caller agreement requirement greater than 11
:::

## Cell line evaluation

:::{.center}
- 56 cell lines
- "Wisdom of crowds" defines TP & FP
:::

![](./img/fusion_bench-4a.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- To evaluate on cancer cell line data with unknown true fusions
- They let caller agreement threshold vary from 1,...,23 and compute TP and FP for each case -> perf. dist.
- Takeaway i): again STAR-Fusion and Arriba perform the best (raw read aligners) while assembly methods perform worst (Trinity)
- Takeaway ii): Top and bottom rankings hardly vary as caller agreement threshold changes, but middle rankings do change
:::

## Runtime

![](./img/fusion_bench-4b.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- In terms of runtime,
- Pizzly, STAR, and Arriba are also fastest alongside having high classification perf.
- However, STAR 'kickstart' is officially no longer supported/recommended as of today
:::

## Cell line evaluation

![](./img/fusion_bench-4d.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- At caller agreement = 7 definition of TP and FP,
- STAR-Fusion has both high precision and recall. Arriba is a close second
- The assembly-based mehods have high precision, but low recall.
:::

## Fusion benchmark summary

:::{.center}
1. Raw read mapping methods outperform transcript assembly methods
2. STAR-Fusion and Arriba are top-performers
3. Similar results for simulated and cell line evaluation

## STAR-Fusion pipeline

![](./img/star_fusion-1.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- STAR-Fusion is conceptually simple
- All rna-seq reads are aligned to reference
- Count discordant & split reads involving genes
- Apply various filters
:::

## STAR-Fusion filters


:::{.center}
:::{.small}
- Split read min. alignment size (25bp each)
- Ignore minority breakpoint contributers
- Homology
- "Promiscuous" genes (many fusion partners)
:::
:::

![](./img/star_fusion-1.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Filters include 
- Split read min. alignment size
- Ignore minority breakpoint contributors, after defining a main breakpoint cluster
- Homology
- Promiscuous genes that have many fusion partners
:::

## Evaluation

:::{.center}
![](./img/star_fusion-2ab.png){fig-align="center" width="60%"}
![](./img/star_fusion-3ab.png){fig-align="center" width="60%"}
:::


:::notes
- Same simul. and cell line data was used for evaluation. Similar results
:::

## Research gaps

:::{.center}

1. Recurrent fusion caller over multiple samples
2. Resolving fusions as DNA/RNA driven

:::

:::notes
- Again, I think calling over multiple samples has 2 advantages
- i) fusions in multiple tumor samples implies the fusion is more likely to be a common driver
- ii) calling over multiple samples jointly increases the total fusion signal which would increase sensitivity to sub-clonal fusions that may be overlooked by single sample callers
- And as we've seen fusions can occur in different ways, so resolving the underlying mechanism is useful and essential for accurate detection
:::

## Samplot

:::{.center}
Sections

1. Samplot examples
2. VCF support
3. Image-driven SV filtering
:::

:::notes
- samplot is designed specifically for viewing structural variants from alignment data
- the paper covers
- example samplots for various SV types
- an interactive VCF mode
- and automated SV false positive filtering using a CNN trained on samplot images
:::

## DEL

![](./img/samplot-1.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Samplot Uses tracks to view multiple forms of SV evidence
- Track 1: short-read seq alignments
- Alignment tracks directly show SV evidence at high resolution
  - Connected squares are discordant paired-end reads
  - Dashed lines are split reads
  - Grey background distribution is coverage (reads aligned per base)
- Track 2: long-read seq alignments also supported
- Track 3 and 4: annotation tracks are supported, such as repeats and gene transcripts
:::

## DUP and INV


![](./img/samplot-2.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- The first fig. was a DEL, but samplot can delineate other SV types
- a) DUP: inc. cov. & reads mapping from copy 1 to copy 2
- b) INV: reads where reverse strand mate aligns before forward strand (abnormal) shown in blue
- c) INV translocation: Blue read pairs spanning CHR 2 to CHR X
:::

## VCF browser

![](./img/samplot-3.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Often, variants need to be compared across samples, such as a VCF
- View multiple variants easily using tabular interface and multiple samples per plot
:::

## Automated filtering

![](./img/samplot-4.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Idea: use samplot images for automated filtering of variant calls
- A CNN was trained on samplot images to indicate true/false call
- Experiment: DEL SV calls in short-read; use long-read verified SVs as truth
- Dec. TP  means incorrectly filtered SV
- Dec. FP means correctly filtered out SV
- Compared against a rule-based method (duphold), SVM classifier (SV2), and ParaGraph (graph-based method)
- Takeaway: samplot and duphold best retain TPs while reducing FPs
- Takeaway d): A long-read model also effectively filtered out some FPs while retaining most TPs
:::

## Generalization

![](./img/samplot-5a.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- To see how samplot-ml genearlizes to other datasets and different seq. parameters, compared two seq runs of HG002.
- Takeaway: Filtering is still performant in non-training samples and across different seq. params: COV and read length
:::

## Low allele freqency scenarios

![](./img/samplot-5bc.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Variants can be at lower frequencies than expected by heterozygosity due to mosaicism (subset of cells) or somaticism (mixed-tumor-normal)
- Experiment: in-silico mixing two samples to various allele ratios and see how many TPs are still retained after filtering
- Takeaway: samplot substantially outperforms SV2 and slightly outperforms duphold, particularly when SVs are at lower allele frequencies
:::

## What causes endogenous SVs?

:::{.center}


<br>

**Homology**

ATCGATCG **Seq. 1**
<br>
AACGAACG **Seq. 2**

<br>

**Repeats**

TAAAAAAT **Seq. 1**
<br>
CAAAAAAT **Seq. 2**


:::

::: notes
"Repeats" -> "replication failures".
"Homology" -> "recombination"
:::

## NAHR summary

<br>

:::{.center}

- Recombination at homologous, but non-matching loci
- Breakpoints have large homology
- Example: Smith-Magenis syndrome
- Relatively high reurrency

:::


## Temple syndrome

:::{.center}

<br>

- BIR SV: CHR 14 DUP
- Symptoms
  - Intellectual disabilities
  - Early onset puberty

:::

## BIR summary

- Replication template switching due to microhomology
- Breakpoints show microhomology
- Example: Temple syndrome; CHR 14 DUP-TRP/INV-DUP
- Low recurrency

## Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease

<br>

:::{.center}

- Mechanism: CHR X DUP; PLP1 gene
- Symptoms:
  - Involuntary movements
  - Developmental delays
:::

## FoSTeS summary

:::{.center}

<br>

- Template switching from one replication fork to another
- Breakpoints have microhomology
- Example: Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease
- Low recurrency

:::

## Complexity of 1bp context SNVs

:::{.center}

<br>

- gnomAD considers SNVs with 1bp context
  - A**C**G -> A**A**G OR A**T**G OR A**G**G
- $4^3=64$ possible 3-mers
- 3 possible SNVs per 3-mer
- Total 3-mer SNVs is $64\cdot 3=192$



:::
